nationality_or_literary_tradition: Saint Lucian; poet and playwright writing in English and Saint Lucian Creole, resident for long periods in Trinidad and the United States
literary_identity: Saint Lucian poet and playwright, Nobel laureate, who made the Caribbean archipelago the matter of an epic poetry in English and Creole, from In a Green Night to Omeros
biography: Derek Alton Walcott was born on 23 January 1930 in Castries, Saint Lucia, the son of Warwick Walcott, a civil servant and sometime watercolourist who died when Derek was a year old, and Alix Maarlin, a teacher who ran a school in their house and recited poetry to her children. A twin, he was educated at Saint Mary's College in Castries and at the University College of the West Indies in Jamaica, taking a degree in 1953. He published his first poems in a private pamphlet at eighteen, founded the Saint Lucia Arts Guild in 1950, and made his name with the play Henri Christophe (1950) and the collection In a Green Night: Poems 1948-1960 (1962). He lived and taught in Trinidad from 1959 to 1976, founded the Trinidad Theatre Workshop in 1959 and wrote the plays of Dream on Monkey Mountain and Other Plays (1970); his poetry went on through The Castaway (1965), The Gulf (1969), Another Life (1973), Sea Grapes (1976), The Star-Apple Kingdom (1979), The Fortunate Traveller (1981) and Midsummer (1984) to the epic Omeros (1990), which many critics regard as his masterpiece. He was professor of poetry and creative writing at Boston University from 1981 to 2007. He received the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1992, the T. S. Eliot Prize in 2011 for White Egrets, and died at Cap Estate, Saint Lucia, on 17 March 2017.
literary_profile: Poetry: 25 Poems (1948), Epitaph for the Young (1949), Poems (1951), In a Green Night (1962), Selected Poems (1964), The Castaway (1965), The Gulf (1969), Another Life (1973), Sea Grapes (1976), The Star-Apple Kingdom (1979), The Fortunate Traveller (1981), Midsummer (1984), The Arkansas Testament (1987), Omeros (1990), The Bounty (1997), Tiepolo's Hound (2000), The Prodigal (2004), Selected Poems (2007) and White Egrets (2010). Plays: Henri Christophe (1950), The Sea at Dauphin (1954), Dream on Monkey Mountain (1970), The Joker of Seville and O Babylon! (1978) and Remembrance and Pantomime (1980). Essays: What the Twilight Says (1998).
stylistic_characteristics: Long, meditative, densely metaphorical poems in a syntactically elaborate English, set against the plain vernacular speech of Creole characters (Shabine, Achille); the hexameters and terza rima of Omeros; a habit of reading the Caribbean landscape through Homer, Dante and the Bible without letting the classical frame master it; the poet as painter, making and unmaking his island.
intellectual_concerns: Colonial history and the Middle Passage; the divided self of the Caribbean artist ('I have Dutch, nigger, and English in me, and either I'm nobody, or I'm a nation'); the sea, the fishermen and the landscape of Saint Lucia; exile and return; love, age and mortality (White Egrets); the vocation of poetry itself.
historical_significance: The foremost poet of the anglophone Caribbean, who with Omeros gave the region its epic and in doing so reopened the epic as a living form for postcolonial writing; Nobel laureate in 1992 and the model for two generations of Caribbean poets.
bibliographical_notes: Books, from Wikipedia and the Oxford Research Encyclopedia, with the contents of Selected Poems: the collections from 25 Poems (1948) to White Egrets (2010) and the main plays. Installment 10 records only the four Norton selections, 'A Far Cry from Africa' (collected 1962), 'The Schooner Flight' (1979), 'The Season of Phantasmal Peace' (1981) and Omeros (1990), so the bibliography is incomplete; the plays have no records and the date of first publication of 'A Far Cry from Africa' is given as 1962, the date of the collection.

nationality_or_literary_tradition: English; poet, translator and children's writer, Poet Laureate 1984-1998
literary_identity: English poet of the animal and the elemental, Poet Laureate from 1984, whose sequences Wodwo and Crow and the late Birthday Letters changed the sound of postwar English verse
biography: Edward James Hughes was born on 17 August 1930 at Mytholmroyd, in the Calder Valley of West Yorkshire, the youngest of the three children of Edith Farrar and William Henry Hughes, a joiner who had survived the First World War and ran a shop in the village. The family moved to Mexborough, in South Yorkshire, when he was seven, and the landscape of millstone grit and moorland of his childhood remained the ground of his poetry. He read English at Pembroke College, Cambridge, where he met Sylvia Plath, whom he married in 1956; they lived in the United States and then in Devon, and she killed herself in 1963. His first collection, The Hawk in the Rain (1957), won the New York Poetry Center's first publication award and made his name; Lupercal (1960) and Wodwo (1967) followed, and Crow (1970), the sequence of poems about a trickster bird, became his most influential book. He wrote the radio play Under Milk Wood's successor in his own idiom, the children's book The Iron Man (1968), and many volumes of translations and of poems for children; Gaudete (1977), Cave Birds (1978), Moortown (1979) and River (1983) came before he was appointed Poet Laureate in 1984. His later books include Flowers and Insects (1986), Wolfwatching (1989), the Ovid translations of Tales from Ovid (1997) and Birthday Letters (1998), the poems to Plath. He died in London on 28 October 1998.
literary_profile: Poetry: The Hawk in the Rain (1957), Lupercal (1960), Wodwo (1967), Crow (1970), Gaudete (1977), Cave Birds (1978), Moortown (1979), River (1983), Flowers and Insects (1986), Wolfwatching (1989), Rain-Charm for the Duchy (1992), New Selected Poems 1957-1994 (1995), Tales from Ovid (1997) and Birthday Letters (1998); Collected Poems, ed. Paul Keegan (2003). Plays and prose: The Iron Man (1968), Seneca's Oedipus (1969), Shakespeare and the Goddess of Complete Being (1992) and Winter Pollen (1994).
stylistic_characteristics: A poetry of hard stresses and dense consonantal sound, built on the cadence of Anglo-Saxon and of Hughes's Yorkshire speech; violent, exact imagery of animals, weather and machinery; repetitive, chant-like sequences in Crow and Cave Birds; the late poems in Birthday Letters plainer, quieter and more colloquial.
intellectual_concerns: The violence and energy of the natural world (hawks, pike, wind, the moor); the brute fact of animal existence as a rebuke to human consciousness; myth, folklore and the occult (Crow, Cave Birds, Gaudete); the First World War and the Yorkshire landscape of his childhood (Moortown, Remains of Elmet); marriage, bereavement and memory (Birthday Letters).
historical_significance: The dominant English poet of his generation and, as Poet Laureate from 1984, the public face of poetry in Britain for fourteen years; Crow and the animal poems changed the register of postwar English verse, and Birthday Letters became one of the best-selling and most discussed volumes of poetry of the century.
bibliographical_notes: Books, from Wikipedia, the Faber Collected Poems contents and general knowledge: the collections from The Hawk in the Rain (1957) to Birthday Letters (1998), with the plays and prose. Installment 10 records only the six Norton selections ('Wind', 1957; 'Pike', 1960; 'Out' and 'Theology', 1967; 'Crow's Last Stand' and 'Crow Tyrannosaurus', 1970), so the bibliography is incomplete; the books have no records and the children's books were not checked.

nationality_or_literary_tradition: Nigerian; novelist, poet, critic and essayist writing in English
literary_identity: Nigerian novelist whose Things Fall Apart gave modern African literature its founding book and whose later fiction and essays carried the argument about the African writer, colonialism and the English language
biography: Albert Chinualumogu Achebe was born on 16 November 1930 in Ogidi, in the Igbo country of eastern Nigeria, the son of Isaiah Okafo Achebe, a teacher and evangelist of the Church Missionary Society, and Janet Anaenechi Iloegbunam; he grew up between the mission and the traditional religion of his grandfather's generation. He was educated at the Government College in Umuahia and at the University College, Ibadan, where he read English and became critical of the way Western literature represented Africa. He taught briefly and joined the Nigerian Broadcasting Service in Lagos in 1954; Things Fall Apart appeared in 1958, followed by No Longer at Ease (1960), Arrow of God (1964) and A Man of the People (1966). He was a founder and the first editor of the Heinemann African Writers Series. During the Biafran war (1967-1970) he supported Biafran independence and worked for its cause abroad; the poems of Beware, Soul Brother (1971) and the stories of Girls at War (1972) came out of the war, and his essay collection Morning Yet on Creation Day (1975) includes 'The Novelist as Teacher' and his reply to Conrad, 'An Image of Africa' (1975). A car crash in 1990 left him partly paralysed and he moved to the United States, teaching at Bard College and, from 2009, at Brown University. Anthills of the Savannah (1987) was his last novel. He won the Man Booker International Prize in 2007 and died in Boston on 21 March 2013.
literary_profile: Novels: Things Fall Apart (1958), No Longer at Ease (1960), Arrow of God (1964), A Man of the People (1966) and Anthills of the Savannah (1987). Stories: The Sacrificial Egg (1962), Girls at War and Other Stories (1972) and African Short Stories (1985, edited with C. L. Innes). Poetry: Beware, Soul Brother (1971) and Collected Poems (2004). Essays: Morning Yet on Creation Day (1975), Hopes and Impediments (1988), The Education of a British-Protected Child (2009) and There Was a Country (2012). Children's books: Chike and the River (1966), How the Leopard Got His Claws (1972) and The Flute (1977).
stylistic_characteristics: A plain, measured English that carries the rhythm and idiom of Igbo speech, built out of proverbs, folk-tales and the cadences of the King James Bible; an ironic narrative manner that lets a community's own language judge its actions; the mature novels combine a large historical span with a tight, dramatic scene; the stories of the war are short, bare and unsparing.
intellectual_concerns: The collision of Igbo tradition and colonial Christianity (Things Fall Apart); the corruption and disillusionment of independence (No Longer at Ease, A Man of the People); the Biafran war and its aftermath (Girls at War, 'Civil Peace'); the responsibility of the African writer and the politics of language; masculinity, gender and the exercise of power in the Igbo world.
historical_significance: The founding novel of modern African literature in English, translated into more than fifty languages and taught across the world; Achebe is called the father of modern African writing, a title he rejected, and his essays on Conrad and on the African writer set the terms of the postcolonial debate about the English language and the African novel.
bibliographical_notes: Books, from Wikipedia's list and general knowledge: the five novels, the story collections, the poetry and essay collections and the children's books listed. Installment 10 records only the Norton selection, 'Civil Peace' (1971), so the bibliography is incomplete; the novels, which would have their own records in a complete bibliography of the author, are not recorded here, and the dates of the essay collections were not checked title by title.

nationality_or_literary_tradition: Trinidadian-born British; novelist, travel writer and essayist writing in English
literary_identity: Trinidadian-born Nobel laureate whose novels of Trinidad, Africa, India and England, from A House for Mr Biswas to The Enigma of Arrival, and whose travel books made him the century's most exact and most contested chronicler of displacement
biography: Vidiadhar Surajprasad Naipaul was born on 17 August 1932 in Chaguanas, Trinidad, into a family of Indian brahmin descent; his father, Seepersad Naipaul, was a journalist and short-story writer, and the household's poverty and his father's ambitions are the matter of the early books. He won a scholarship to Queen's Royal College in Port of Spain and another, in 1950, to University College, Oxford, where he read English; he graduated in 1953 and lived in London from 1954, writing for the BBC Caribbean Service and reviewing. His first three novels, The Mystic Masseur (1957), The Suffrage of Elvira (1958) and Miguel Street (1959), were comedies of Trinidadian life; A House for Mr Biswas (1961) made his name. A visit to India in 1962 produced An Area of Darkness (1964), the first of the travel books that include The Middle Passage (1962), The Loss of El Dorado (1969), India: A Wounded Civilization (1977), Among the Believers (1981), Finding the Centre (1984), The Enigma of Arrival (1987), India: A Million Mutinies Now (1990) and Beyond Belief (1998). His later novels include The Mimic Men (1967), In a Free State (1971, Booker Prize), Guerrillas (1975), A Bend in the River (1979), The Enigma of Arrival, A Way in the World (1994), Half a Life (2001) and Magic Seeds (2004). He was knighted in 1990, received the Nobel Prize in Literature in 2001 and died in London on 11 August 2018.
literary_profile: Novels: The Mystic Masseur (1957), The Suffrage of Elvira (1958), Miguel Street (1959), A House for Mr Biswas (1961), Mr Stone and the Knights Companion (1963), The Mimic Men (1967), In a Free State (1971), Guerrillas (1975), A Bend in the River (1979), The Enigma of Arrival (1987), A Way in the World (1994), Half a Life (2001) and Magic Seeds (2004). Travel and essays: The Middle Passage (1962), An Area of Darkness (1964), The Loss of El Dorado (1969), India: A Wounded Civilization (1977), Among the Believers (1981), Finding the Centre (1984), A Turn in the South (1989), India: A Million Mutinies Now (1990), Beyond Belief (1998) and The Writer and the World (2003).
stylistic_characteristics: A precise, unhurried, declarative prose, with a journalist's eye for the revealing detail and a satirist's ear for Trinidadian speech; the travel books combine reportage, memoir and portrait; the later novels replace plot with meditation and the essayistic sequence, and the sentence grows longer and more qualified as the books proceed.
intellectual_concerns: Displacement and the search for a home (Mr Biswas's house, the narrator of The Enigma of Arrival); the colonial aftermath in Trinidad, Africa and India; the fragility of newly independent states and the predicament of the mimic man; the writer's exile and the immigrant's self-invention; order, dignity and the small decencies against disorder.
historical_significance: One of the two or three most important novelists in English of the postwar period, and the most influential travel writer in the language; his work is central to postcolonial criticism, both as its subject and as its provocation, and the Nobel citation praised his 'incorruptible scrutiny' and his 'uncompromising scrutiny of the effects of colonialism'.
bibliographical_notes: The books are listed from Wikipedia's article and general knowledge, in order of first publication; only the Norton selection, 'One Out of Many' (in In a Free State, 1971), has a work record, so the bibliography is incomplete. The travel books and later novels have no records, and the dates of first publication were not checked title by title against a bibliography.

nationality_or_literary_tradition: Nigerian; playwright, poet, novelist and essayist, writing in English with Yoruba and Nigerian idiom, resident for long periods in Britain and the United States
literary_identity: Nigerian playwright and Nobel laureate whose plays, from A Dance of the Forests to Death and the King's Horseman and The Road, fuse Yoruba ritual, myth and masquerade with the forms of European drama
biography: Akinwande Oluwole Soyinka was born on 13 July 1934 in Abeokuta, in western Nigeria, the son of Samuel Ayodele Soyinka, a schoolteacher and Anglican, and Grace Eniola Soyinka, a trader and activist in the women's movement of Abeokuta; he grew up in the mission compound of Aké, which he later described in Aké: The Years of Childhood (1981). He attended Government College, Ibadan, and University College, Ibadan, and in 1954 went to the University of Leeds, where he took a degree in English and wrote a thesis on the drama of the absurd. He returned to Nigeria in 1960 and founded the 1960 Masks and then the Orisun Theatre, writing and directing plays that drew on Yoruba masquerade and ritual; his early plays include The Swamp Dwellers (1958), The Lion and the Jewel (1959), A Dance of the Forests (1960, for the independence celebrations), The Strong Breed (1964), The Road (1965) and Kongi's Harvest (1967). During the Nigerian Civil War he was arrested and held in solitary confinement for nearly two years (1967-1969), an experience recorded in The Man Died (1972). Later plays include Madmen and Specialists (1971), Death and the King's Horseman (1975), Opera Wonyosi (1981), A Play of Giants (1984), and The Beatification of Area Boy (1995); his novels are The Interpreters (1965), Season of Anomy (1973) and Chronicles from the Land of the Happiest People on Earth (2021). He was awarded the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1986, the first African writer to receive it, and he has taught at Cambridge, Yale, Emory and Oxford.
literary_profile: Plays: The Swamp Dwellers (1958), The Lion and the Jewel (1959), A Dance of the Forests (1960), The Strong Breed (1964), The Road (1965), Kongi's Harvest (1967), Madmen and Specialists (1971), Death and the King's Horseman (1975), Opera Wonyosi (1981), A Play of Giants (1984) and The Beatification of Area Boy (1995). Novels: The Interpreters (1965), Season of Anomy (1973) and Chronicles from the Land of the Happiest People on Earth (2021). Poetry: Idanre and Other Poems (1967), A Shuttle in the Crypt (1972), Ogun Abibiman (1976), Mandela's Earth (1988) and Samarkand (1990). Memoirs and essays: The Man Died (1972), Myth, Literature and the African World (1976), Aké (1981), Art, Dialogue and Outrage (1988) and You Must Set Forth at Dawn (2006).
stylistic_characteristics: A theatre of total performance in which Yoruba ritual, drumming, dance, masquerade and the language of the market are set against the conventions of the European stage; a dense, punning, rhetorical English, often drawing on Yoruba proverbs and idiom; satire and farce alongside tragedy; plays built on processions, interruptions and the eruption of the supernatural into everyday life.
intellectual_concerns: The encounter of Yoruba traditional religion and culture with colonialism, Christianity and modernity; ritual sacrifice and the burden of the past (Death and the King's Horseman); political corruption and dictatorship in post-independence Africa (Kongi's Harvest, Madmen and Specialists); the artist's and the individual's relation to the community; memory, tyranny and exile.
historical_significance: The central figure of modern African drama in English, the first African Nobel laureate in literature, and a writer whose work joined African performance traditions to world theatre; Death and the King's Horseman is regarded as his masterpiece and as one of the great plays of the twentieth century.
bibliographical_notes: Plays, novels, poems and memoirs are listed from Wikipedia's article and general knowledge; only the Norton selection, Death and the King's Horseman (1975), has a work record, so the bibliography is incomplete. The dates of the earlier plays are those of first performance rather than publication and were not checked against a bibliography.

literary_identity: English playwright whose formally inventive plays, from Cloud 9 and Top Girls to Serious Money and Far Away, made her the most innovative political dramatist of the postwar British stage
biography: Caryl Lesley Churchill was born on 3 September 1938 in Finsbury, London, and grew up in Montreal and in Oxfordshire, where her family moved during the war. She read English at Lady Margaret Hall, Oxford, where she wrote two plays produced by student societies, and married David Harter in 1961, with whom she had three sons. Her first professional work was for radio, and her stage plays of the 1970s - Owners (1972), Objections to Sex and Violence (1976), Light Shining in Buckinghamshire (1976) and Vinegar Tom (1976) - were written for the fringe and for the Royal Court, the last two in collaboration with the feminist theatre company Monstrous Regiment. Cloud 9 (1979) and Top Girls (1982) made her reputation; they were followed by Fen (1983), Serious Money (1987, a satire in rhyming couplets on the City of London), Icecream (1989), The Skriker (1994), Blue Heart (1997), Far Away (2000), A Number (2002), Drunk Enough to Say I Love You? (2006), Seven Jewish Children (2009), Love and Information (2012), Here We Go (2015), Escaped Alone (2016) and What If If Only (2021). She has worked throughout with the director Max Stafford-Clark and with the Royal Court, and her plays are characterised by non-naturalistic devices: overlapping dialogue, doubling, time-shifts and abrupt shifts of register.
literary_profile: Plays: Owners (1972), Objections to Sex and Violence (1976), Light Shining in Buckinghamshire (1976), Vinegar Tom (1976), Cloud 9 (1979), Top Girls (1982), Fen (1983), Softcops (1984), Serious Money (1987), Icecream (1989), Mad Forest (1990), The Skriker (1994), Blue Heart (1997), Far Away (2000), A Number (2002), Drunk Enough to Say I Love You? (2006), Seven Jewish Children (2009), Love and Information (2012), Here We Go (2015), Escaped Alone (2016) and What If If Only (2021).
stylistic_characteristics: Non-naturalistic structure: overlapping dialogue, scenes played simultaneously, characters doubled and cross-cast, time-schemes that collide (Cloud 9 moves from Victorian Africa to 1979 London with the same characters aged by only twenty-five years); verse and rhyming couplets in Serious Money; short, elliptical scenes and abrupt reversals; language pared down to fragments in the late plays.
intellectual_concerns: The abuses of power, political and sexual (Top Girls, Serious Money); sexual politics and the construction of gender (Cloud 9, Vinegar Tom); women's history and the cost of success; Thatcherism, the City and the market (Top Girls, Serious Money); war, torture and complicity (Far Away, Seven Jewish Children); the fragility of language and of the family (A Number, Escaped Alone).
historical_significance: The most important British playwright of her generation and, in the 2011 Village Voice poll of dramatists, the greatest living playwright; her formal inventions changed the possibilities of political theatre in Britain, and Top Girls and Cloud 9 are among the most frequently revived plays of the postwar repertoire.
bibliographical_notes: The plays are listed from Wikipedia's article and general knowledge; only the Norton selection, Top Girls (1982), has a work record, so the bibliography is incomplete. Dates are those of first production, which for Churchill's plays is usually the significant date, and were not checked one by one against a bibliography.

birthplace: Tamniaran, near Castledawson, County Londonderry, Northern Ireland
nationality_or_literary_tradition: Irish; poet, translator and playwright, resident in Dublin from 1976, writing in English
literary_identity: Irish poet and Nobel laureate whose poems of the Mossbawn farm, the Troubles and the ordinary world, from Death of a Naturalist to Human Chain, made him the most widely read poet in English of his time
biography: Seamus Justin Heaney was born on 13 April 1939 at Mossbawn, the family farm in the townland of Tamniaran near Castledawson, County Londonderry, the eldest of the nine children of Patrick Heaney, a cattle dealer, and Margaret Kathleen McCann. The family moved to Bellaghy when he was a boy. He was educated at the local primary school and at St Columb's College in Derry, then read English at Queen's University Belfast, graduating in 1961; he trained as a teacher and lectured at St Joseph's College in Belfast and at Queen's, where he encountered the poetry of Ted Hughes and began to publish. Death of a Naturalist (1966) made his name, and was followed by Door into the Dark (1969), Wintering Out (1972), North (1975), Field Work (1979), Station Island (1984), The Haw Lantern (1987), Seeing Things (1991), The Spirit Level (1996), Electric Light (2001), District and Circle (2006) and Human Chain (2010), with the translations of Sweeney Astray (1983), The Cure at Troy (1990), Beowulf (1999) and Aeneid VI (2016). He moved to Dublin in 1976 and taught at Harvard from 1981 and at Oxford as Professor of Poetry from 1989 to 1994. He received the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1995 and died in Dublin on 30 August 2013.
literary_profile: Poetry: Death of a Naturalist (1966), Door into the Dark (1969), Wintering Out (1972), North (1975), Field Work (1979), Station Island (1984), The Haw Lantern (1987), Seeing Things (1991), The Spirit Level (1996), Electric Light (2001), District and Circle (2006) and Human Chain (2010); Opened Ground: Selected Poems 1966-1996 (1998). Translations: Sweeney Astray (1983), The Cure at Troy (1990), Beowulf (1999) and Aeneid VI (2016). Plays: The Cure at Troy and The Burial at Thebes (2004). Essays: Preoccupations (1980), The Government of the Tongue (1988) and Finders Keepers (2002).
stylistic_characteristics: A poetry of the senses and of the soil, with a strong stress metre and a rich consonantal music; exact description of farm work, bogland and weather; the sonnet sequences and the longer meditative poems; a diction that holds Latinate abstraction and Ulster dialect together; the translations, especially Beowulf, carry the same muscular line.
intellectual_concerns: The labour and inheritance of the family farm (Digging, Follower); the Troubles and the poet's responsibility in the face of violence (North, Punishment, Casualty); the bog bodies and the archaeology of the past; place, soil and the names of places; the ordinary epiphanies of the later poems; memory, the dead and the consolations of the everyday.
historical_significance: The best-known and most widely read poet in English of the late twentieth century, praised by Robert Lowell as 'the most important Irish poet since Yeats'; his Nobel Prize in 1995 recognised a body of work that entered school syllabuses and public life without losing its formal ambition, and his death was treated as a national event in Ireland.
bibliographical_notes: The collections are listed from Wikipedia, the Ricorso bibliography and general knowledge, with the contents of Death of a Naturalist (1966), North (1975), Field Work (1979) and Station Island (1984) checked against the Ricorso listing. Installment 10 records only the six dated Norton selections ('Digging', 1966; 'The Grauballe Man' and 'Punishment', 1975; 'Casualty', 1979; station Island XII, 1984; 'Clearances', 1987); the bibliography is therefore incomplete, and the translations and prose have no records.

literary_identity: Canadian short-story writer and Nobel laureate whose stories of small-town Ontario and of women's lives, from Dance of the Happy Shades to Dear Life, remade the short story as a form of long, retrospective knowledge
biography: Alice Ann Laidlaw was born on 10 July 1931 on a fox farm outside Wingham, in Huron County, Ontario, the daughter of Robert Laidlaw, a fox farmer who later worked as a foundry labourer and watchman, and Anne Clarke, a schoolteacher. She read English at the University of Western Ontario, where she spent two years, and married James Munro in 1951, moving with him to Vancouver, where she ran a bookshop and began publishing stories in Canadian periodicals. Her first collection, Dance of the Happy Shades, appeared in 1968 and won the Governor General's Award; it was followed by Lives of Girls and Women (1971), a sequence of linked stories that reads as a novel, Something I've Been Meaning to Tell You (1974), Who Do You Think You Are? (1978), The Moons of Jupiter (1982), The Progress of Love (1986), Friend of My Youth (1990), Open Secrets (1994), The Love of a Good Woman (1998), Hateship, Friendship, Courtship, Loveship, Marriage (2001), Runaway (2004), The View from Castle Rock (2006), Too Much Happiness (2009) and Dear Life (2012). She separated from her first husband and lived from the 1970s with Gerald Fremlin in Clinton, Ontario, and in Comox, British Columbia. She won the Man Booker International Prize in 2009 and the Nobel Prize in Literature in 2013, and died at Port Hope, Ontario, on 13 May 2024.
literary_profile: Stories: Dance of the Happy Shades (1968), Something I've Been Meaning to Tell You (1974), Who Do You Think You Are? (1978), The Moons of Jupiter (1982), The Progress of Love (1986), Friend of My Youth (1990), Open Secrets (1994), The Love of a Good Woman (1998), Hateship, Friendship, Courtship, Loveship, Marriage (2001), Runaway (2004), The View from Castle Rock (2006), Too Much Happiness (2009) and Dear Life (2012). Lives of Girls and Women (1971) is a sequence of linked stories. Selected Stories appeared in 1996 and Family Furnishings: Selected Stories 1995-2014 in 2014.
stylistic_characteristics: Plain, unhurried prose that moves freely in time, beginning in the middle or near the end of a life and working back; the reveal withheld until the last paragraph; a narrator who is often a woman looking back at a girl's misunderstanding; the ordinary Ontario small town rendered with documentary exactness and no condescension.
intellectual_concerns: The gap between what a child or a young woman understands and what has actually happened; sex, marriage and the unequal arrangements between men and women; class and respectability in small-town Ontario; the work of memory and the way a life is revised in the telling; the natural world and the farm as a place of labour and of casual cruelty.
historical_significance: The most important writer of short stories in English in the second half of the twentieth century, and the first Canadian to win the Nobel Prize in Literature; her stories are credited with widening the form's capacity for time, memory and moral ambiguity, and she is the standard against which later short-story writers in English are measured.
bibliographical_notes: The list of collections is taken from Wikipedia and general knowledge and checked against the published volumes' titles and dates; only the Norton selection, 'Walker Brothers Cowboy' (in Dance of the Happy Shades, 1968), has a work record, so the bibliography is incomplete. The stories themselves are not recorded individually, and no text of them was consulted beyond the summaries cited for the Norton story.
